headline: Under 90 days?
Pay nobody.
coverSpec.title: A decision rule for whether paying for US visa appointment help is worth it
coverSpec.desc: Below about 90 days of queue at your post, the free routes are enough and nobody should be paying anyone. Between about 90 and 180 days it depends on how wide a range of dates you can accept and how much of your own time you can spend. Above about 180 days with a fixed deadline is where a paid option earns its place. The two genuinely free routes are working the calendar yourself and the expedited appointment request on documented urgency.

faq.q: Is it worth paying for a US visa appointment service?
faq.a: It depends almost entirely on how long the queue at your post is and how fixed your travel dates are. Below roughly 90 days, the free routes will usually get you there and paying anyone is poor value. Above roughly 180 days with a deadline you cannot move, a paid option starts to make sense. In between it turns on whether you can spend your own time watching a portal and how wide a date range you can accept.

faq.q: What are the genuinely free ways to get an earlier US visa date?
faq.a: Two. Working the calendar yourself, which means holding a confirmed appointment and checking regularly for cancellations, and this is the method the State Department itself points applicants at. And the expedited appointment request, which is free, discretionary and decided on documented urgency: medical emergencies, the funeral of an immediate family member, or a student within 60 days of a programme start date.

faq.q: Do paid services get access to appointments I cannot see?
faq.a: No, and anyone claiming otherwise is describing something that does not exist. There is no separate inventory, no reserved allocation and no back channel. Everyone is looking at the same public calendar. What a paid service can offer is persistence, attention at hours that do not suit you, and judgement about which openings are worth taking. That is a real service, and it is not a hidden supply.

faq.q: Are the free alert websites enough on their own?
faq.a: They can be, if you can act within seconds of a notification at any hour. That is the condition people underestimate. An alert tells you an appointment exists; you still have to be at a device, signed in, with your details ready, before someone else takes it. If your working day makes that impossible, an alert plan bills you every month for information you cannot use.

faq.q: How does the $750 government expedite compare?
faq.a: It is the only fee that reliably moves a date, and it is available almost nowhere. The State Department's pilot runs at Mission Mexico and Mission Canada as of 19 August 2026, covers B-1 and B-2 only, costs $750 per applicant paid up front and non-refundable, and is scheduled to end on 31 December 2026. If you qualify and have a hard deadline, it beats every private option. Most readers do not qualify.

faq.q: What should I never pay for?
faq.a: A slot promised before you have a scheduling account, a DS-160 and a paid application fee, because nothing can be reserved in advance. Any government fee paid to an intermediary rather than through your own consular process. A guarantee of a date or an approval, which nobody outside the US government can give. And a $750 expedite at a post where the pilot does not run.

faq.q: Does paying anyone affect my visa decision?
faq.a: No. Scheduling and adjudication are separate. A consular officer assesses your eligibility on the evidence you present, and how the appointment was booked is not part of that. The one exception worth knowing is that appointments booked in breach of scheduling rules can be cancelled and the applicant's scheduling privileges suspended, which happened to about 2,000 appointments in India in March 2025.

cta.body: That is the whole offer on this page. Send us your post, your current appointment date and the widest range of dates you could accept, and you will get an honest read on whether a paid option makes sense for your case, including when the answer is that it does not. We would rather turn away a case we cannot improve than take a fee for one, and the decision rule above is the same one we apply internally.
